reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes an MEV arbitrage bot with claims of 62.9% Ether profits and win rates of up to 92%. It directs viewers through contract deployment, gas fees, and funding with at least 0.5 Ether, while describing recovery of more than half the deposit within about 24 hours.

citations.quote: Chatgpt MEV Arbitrage Bot Made Me 62.9% Ether Profit (FULL TUTORIAL)
This bot it takes into the Ethereum mempool, search for profitable transactions
i'm going to show you exactly how i build this uniswap trading bot and how to use it
Now we're going to deploy this to our wallet
I recommend funding the contract with at least 0.5 Ether

opening.argument: Judge, the speaker does not present the reported returns as a fixed outcome: he says, “The profits will fluctuate week to week guys.” He also identifies gas as a cost of deployment and warns that a small balance may be consumed by fees. Those qualifications matter when weighing the profit claims. The account is enthusiastic, but its own discussion of variable returns and operating costs supports reading it as a demonstration of a risky trading tool, not a promise that viewers will earn the same amount.

citations.quote: The profits will fluctuate week to week guys.
We need to confirm the contract on the blockchain by paying gas fees.
If you fund the contract with 0.2 ETHER or less and the bot targets another token with high burn fees, the contract will waste a lot of gas fees.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited 62.9% figure is framed as what the bot “Made Me,” not as a stated guarantee to every viewer. Likewise, the recommendation to fund at least 0.5 Ether is explained in terms of gas costs, and the speaker describes greater profit as potential. The prosecution identifies an invitation to try a trading method, but its quotes do not establish a guaranteed return.

citations.quote: Chatgpt MEV Arbitrage Bot Made Me 62.9% Ether Profit (FULL TUTORIAL)
I recommend funding the contract with at least 0.5 Ether to make sure that won't happen.
potentially more profit you can accumulate over time.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A fluctuation warning does not neutralize the pitch. The speaker recommends putting at least 0.5 Ether into the contract, connects larger deposits to potentially greater profit, and reports gaining more than half his deposit back in about 24 hours. The wrong-side argument shows that returns are not expressly guaranteed; it does not account for how strongly the video encourages viewers to fund the bot on the strength of exceptional claimed results.

citations.quote: I recommend funding the contract with at least 0.5 Ether
Keep in mind that the more you put in the larger the trades you'll be able to make, and potentially more profit you can accumulate over time.
it basically took me 24 hours to gain over half of my deposit back

opening.argument: Judge, the video gives a concrete smart-contract walkthrough. The speaker says he will show how he built the bot and how to use it, then walks through matching the Solidity compiler version, deploying through Remix, and inspecting the contract's start and withdraw functions. That operational sequence is substantial, not merely a profit claim. The reported result appears within a tutorial that shows the tools and steps the speaker says he used; it need not be treated as an independently verified outcome to recognize the video's instructional content.

citations.quote: i'm going to show you exactly how i build this uniswap trading bot and how to use it
Under a compiler select the 0.6.6 version, so that it matches our contract.
Head over to the Deploy and Run Transactions tab in Remix.
Start enables the bot to start monitoring the mempool smart contract start enables the bot to start monitoring the Mempool and withdraw stops the bot and transfer funds back into your wallet.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution's deployment and funding quotes are also steps in the walkthrough; their presence alone does not settle whether the central purpose is deceptive solicitation. The speaker describes the ether as funding for trading and gas, and points viewers to an external blockchain explorer to check an address. The profit claims warrant scrutiny, but they do not erase the detailed tool demonstration.

citations.quote: Fund it with some ETHER which will be used for trading.
you can follow these addresses using EtherScan

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The tutorial format is precisely how the video moves viewers from a return claim to funding a contract. It recommends at least 0.5 Ether, says more funding can enable larger trades and potentially more profit, and directs viewers to start the bot after funding. Detailed operational steps do not make the profit-led funding pitch incidental.

citations.quote: I recommend funding the contract with at least 0.5 Ether
the more you put in the larger the trades you'll be able to make, and potentially more profit you can accumulate over time.
Last step is to click start.

opening.argument: Judge, the visible transaction flow is a wallet interacting with a deployed smart contract, not a stated payment to the speaker. The walkthrough uses an injected Web3 wallet, describes funding the contract for trading, and says the withdraw function returns funds to the user's wallet. Access to the speaker's private script is conditioned on likes, not described as a purchase. None of that proves the contract works as claimed, but the supplied account does not establish that the speaker receives viewers' ether or asks for their wallet credentials. The narrower reading is a promotional tutorial with unverified performance claims.

citations.quote: Here you want to select the injected web 3 as the environment.
Fund it with some ETHER which will be used for trading.
withdraw stops the bot and transfer funds back into your wallet.
I made the script private so no one else can see it but me however i will share its link once this video gets 1k likes

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution cites a deposit recommendation, but a recommendation to fund a deployed contract does not, by itself, identify who can control that contract or where withdrawals ultimately go. The speaker describes checking the contract balance and then withdrawing to a wallet. Those claims should not be accepted as proof of safety, but the prosecution's quoted steps do not demonstrate a transfer to the speaker.

citations.quote: We can make sure by checking our contract address on the Ether scanned once again. Ensuring our Ether is in the contract.
when you click withdraw, the bot will stop trading and return to total ether you entered initially including the profit back to your wallet.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The claimed withdrawal behavior is the speaker's assertion, not evidence that a viewer's funds are recoverable. The video asks viewers to fund a contract with at least 0.5 Ether, activate it, and expect trading profits; it then portrays a balance exceeding the initial deposit. The absence of a visible payment to the speaker does not resolve the risk created by that funding instruction and return claim.
